title: Metrics Have Roles: Inputs, Outputs, Outcomes, and Guardrails
editorial_note: Opening revised to lead with the lesson itself. Remaining dialogue is an automated editorial draft; review spoken wording and meaning before final publication.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Metrics Have Roles: Inputs, Outputs, Outcomes, and Guardrails.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Inputs describe resources, conditions, and capability available to the system: staffed navigator hours, proportion of clinics connected, research capacity, or referrals with complete data. Inputs enable work but do not prove benefit.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: A metric’s role comes from the decision
turns.text: What changes when we look at a metric’s role comes from the decision?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Outputs describe what the organisation or system produced: clinic records verified, accessibility defects repaired, notifications delivered, or navigator cases handled. Outputs demonstrate delivery, not what changed for people.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Behaviour and service-result measures describe what actors did and what the service fulfilled: patients requested help, clinics accepted referrals, or reroutes completed. They bridge output and outcome but may remain proxies.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Outcomes describe changed states that matter: patients reach appropriate care sooner, staff avoid rework, or access gaps narrow. Outcomes may lag and depend on forces outside the product.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Guardrails protect non-target qualities and stakeholders from unacceptable trade-offs. They can cover safety, accessibility, privacy, trust, workload, latency, error, cost, and distributional harm.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A measure is not permanently one type. Time to appointment is an outcome for a scheduling programme and a guardrail for an explanation experiment. Label role, scope, and decision.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at construct a metric architecture?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Start from a theory of change:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: If we invest in capability/input, we can deliver output, which changes behaviour or service state, which contributes to outcome, provided assumptions hold and guardrails remain acceptable.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: For each link, document owner, population, unit, cadence, lag, source, target or threshold, and rival explanation. Distinguish measures teams can directly influence from outcomes they contribute to. Avoid using an input target as a performance substitute simply because the outcome is slow.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Assign cadences by function. Operational queues may need hourly monitoring, experiment measures daily quality checks, and long-term outcomes quarterly review. Guardrails require an escalation route and authority; observation without response is decoration.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Audit every dashboard tile: What role does it play? Which decision changes? Who owns interpretation? What population and horizon apply? What does it omit? Retire orphan metrics.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: a help centre?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Articles published are output. Searches and opens are behaviour. Problems resolved without repeated effort are outcome. Failed search, inaccessible content, delayed urgent help, and displaced support labour are guardrails. If contact volume falls while unresolved complaints rise, the service has reduced a cost rather than resolved customer problems.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at where this can go wrong?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Activity promotion: research sessions or features shipped become “outcomes.” Role ambiguity: the same number is interpreted differently across teams. Outcome without agency: teams are held to distant results without controllable drivers. Local optimisation: one unit improves its target by transferring work or harm.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Cadence mismatch: slow outcomes are judged daily or urgent guardrails quarterly. Ownerless guardrail: deterioration is visible but nobody can stop rollout.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Build a metric tree from a behavioural theory
turns.text: What changes when we look at build a metric tree from a behavioural theory?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Each metric has definition, population, denominator, event source, time window, segmentation, owner, expected relationship, and decision rule. Diagnostics explain movement; guardrails protect safety, equity, staff load, privacy, and channel shift. A metric without a response is information overhead. A metric with a target but no causal role invites gaming.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The tree represents tensions. Faster request processing can reduce delay while increasing unsuitable transfers; more self-service can reduce calls while excluding people. The team reviews distributions and cohorts, not averages alone, and pairs service data with qualitative evidence. Relationships remain hypotheses until tested.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Metric health is governed too. Instrumentation, definitions, missingness, ownership, and product changes are audited. When a status event changes, historical comparison is annotated or migrated. The dashboard cannot remain more stable than the service semantics beneath it.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: learning platform?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Lessons completed is an output. Demonstrated capability may be an outcome. Time spent can indicate engagement or confusion. A metric tree prevents one convenient event from becoming the educational goal.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Metric architecture is organisation design. It encodes who is accountable, who can act, and whose cost is visible. Senior practitioners resist cascading one metric mechanically through the hierarchy. They preserve shared outcomes while giving teams appropriate leading measures and counter-metrics.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: They also review incentives: once output targets affect performance, people will satisfy them even when the causal link to value breaks.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at build a causal measurement chain?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The chain prevents the team from celebrating activity disconnected from value. If comparison use rises while appropriate resolution does not, the missing link becomes a question. Measures are reviewed for gaming, lag, denominator, and burden before entering a dashboard.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: <! -- Editorial: manual revision; curated product example --

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Illustrative scenario: a language-learning app. Push notifications and lesson starts are inputs; completed practice is an output; retained skill is an outcome. Guardrails watch fatigue, opt-outs, and accessibility. If notifications increase opens but not practice or learning, the team has improved a proxy, not necessarily the experience.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Open a public impact dashboard. Classify each measure. How many describe organisational activity versus changed human outcomes? Which absent guardrail could reverse the story?
